key_insight: Higher interfacial Atwood number makes multi-layer Rayleigh–Taylor instability start sooner, grow faster, and transition from separate mixing layers to a coupled turbulent region.
engineering_relevance: The results help predict and control stratified mixing in thermal, geophysical, and multiphase systems where interface density contrast governs instability and transport.
method: Fully compressible 3D direct numerical simulations with a high-fidelity Navier–Stokes solver.
Ten cases spanning a broad range of interfacial At to compare instability evolution across stratification strengths.
Tracked vorticity, mixing-layer growth, density fluctuations, TKE, and energy partitioning over time.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent onset, quasi-exponential growth, and saturation stages across all cases, with stronger At producing earlier onset, more vorticity, broader mixing regions, and an approximate -11/5 late-stage spectral scaling.
watch_item: Results are specific to the simulated geometry, thermal stratification setup, and parameter range, so extrapolation to other fluids or interface configurations should be done cautiously.
paper_title: Direct numerical simulations of multi-layer Rayleigh-Taylor instability under asymmetric interfacial density stratification
